prompt.context: Your client is an energy firm that has a lot of extra cash and wants to know if they should purchase all the HVAC (heating, ventilation and cooling) service firms in the Atlanta area and consolidate them. The client would like to know if this is a viable investment they should consider.
prompt.question: Should the client acquire and consolidate all HVAC service firms in the Atlanta area? Specifically, will this investment break even within 3 years?

clarifying_info.q: What is the rationale behind this investment?
clarifying_info.a: The client wants to diversify into other industries.

clarifying_info.q: How many HVAC service firms are in the Atlanta area?
clarifying_info.a: There are 500 HVAC service firms in the Atlanta area.

clarifying_info.q: What criteria does the client use to evaluate investments?
clarifying_info.a: The client's finance department requires a 3-year break-even on any investment.

framework: Projected profit from the consolidated entity: estimate current revenue, revenue growth, and any revenue synergies, then identify current cost structure and cost synergies from consolidation
Acquisition price: total capital outlay for buying all 500 firms
Cost of capital: required return used to assess whether the deal meets the 3-year break-even hurdle
Non-financial risks: post-integration issues (cultural differences, management), regulatory issues
Alternatives: if break-even is not met, explore renegotiating price, finding more cost synergies, improving revenue, or seeking other regions/industries

questions.prompt: Walk through the projected revenue of the consolidated entity.
questions.guidance: 500 firms × $10M average annual revenue = $5,000M total revenue. Revenue growth is 3% per year. No revenue synergies because the firms serve the same Atlanta market — no incremental customers are added by consolidation.

math.setup: Total revenue = number of firms × average revenue per firm
steps: Revenue synergies: $0 (same market, no new customers)
math.answer: $5,000M annual revenue with 3% growth and no revenue synergies

questions.prompt: Identify and quantify the current cost structure, then estimate cost synergies from consolidation.
questions.guidance: Current costs are expressed as a % of revenue. Candidate should identify three cost buckets and brainstorm where consolidation creates savings: labor dispatching efficiency, stronger supplier bargaining power on equipment, and consolidation of back-office functions (IT, accounting).

math.setup: Apply cost % to $5,000M revenue to get absolute costs, then apply synergy % to each cost line
math.answer: Total annual cost savings of $197.5M; post-consolidation profit = $447.5M

questions.prompt: Conduct the break-even analysis. Does this investment break even in 3 years?
questions.guidance: Total acquisition cost = 500 × $5M = $2,500M. Simple payback = total investment ÷ annual profit. Also factor in cost of capital (13%) if relevant. Candidate should clearly state whether the 3-year hurdle is met.

math.setup: Break-even (years) = Total acquisition price ÷ Annual post-consolidation profit
steps: Cost of capital check: annual capital cost = 13% × $2,500M = $325M; net annual benefit = $447.5M - $325M = $122.5M; payback on capital-adjusted basis = $2,500M ÷ $122.5M ≈ 20.4 years
Either way, the investment does NOT break even within 3 years
math.answer: Break-even is approximately 5.6 years (simple payback) — the 3-year hurdle is NOT met

brainstorming.prompt: The investment won't break even in 3 years. What options does the client have to improve the payback or pursue value creation differently?

categories.name: Reduce acquisition price
ideas: Negotiate lower per-firm price by leveraging scale (buying all 500 at once)
Assess bargaining power relative to sellers and whether competing bidders exist
Structure earnouts or staged payments to reduce upfront capital outlay

categories.name: Increase cost synergies
ideas: Deeper labor savings beyond 5% through route optimization and scheduling technology
Greater equipment procurement savings by expanding supplier negotiations
Larger admin savings by centralizing more functions (HR, finance, legal)
Energy procurement synergies leveraging the parent's energy firm expertise

categories.name: Improve revenue
ideas: Cross-sell energy services to HVAC customers leveraging parent's portfolio
Advertising efficiency gains from unified brand
Better incentive systems for technicians driving higher throughput
Optimize brand portfolio if some firms have stronger local brand equity

categories.name: Explore alternatives
ideas: Target a subset of Atlanta firms (highest margin ones) rather than all 500
Expand to other metro areas with better market dynamics
Invest in adjacent industries with more attractive return profiles
Joint venture or partial stake instead of full acquisition to reduce capital at risk

recommendation: The acquisition does not meet the client's 3-year break-even requirement — the simple payback is approximately 5.6 years even after capturing all identified cost synergies
We do not recommend proceeding with the deal as currently structured
risks: Post-integration complexity of consolidating 500 independent firms simultaneously (cultural differences, management retention)
Regulatory scrutiny from acquiring 100% of market share in a single metropolitan area
Synergy assumptions may be optimistic — especially labor savings if technicians are already 100% utilized
Revenue growth of 3% may not materialize if the Atlanta HVAC market is cyclical or weather-dependent
next_steps: Negotiate acquisition price down to a level that achieves 3-year break-even (target: ~$1,340M total, or ~$2.7M per firm at $447.5M annual profit over 3 years)
Investigate additional cost synergy levers (technology investment, energy procurement) to close the gap
Model partial acquisition of highest-margin firms to test whether a targeted approach clears the hurdle
Scan other regions and industries for investments that meet the 3-year break-even criterion
